question:
A cultured cell line derives from a single founder cell whose CpG sites were fully methylated on both strands. The maintenance methylation activity is then completely inactivated in all descendants, so hemi-methylated sites are never converted back to fully methylated sites. After the first division after inactivation, every daughter cell carries hemi-methylated DNA at these sites. The culture is then allowed to go through several more divisions.
Over these further divisions, does the overall level of CpG methylation in the culture stay at the level seen after the first division, with no additional loss? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: If methylation patterns are not restored, further cell divisions lead to increased loss of methylation, because the only remaining hemi-methylated DNA strands are those inherited from the last ancestral cell that was fully methylated.
evidence: Further divisions would lead to increased loss as methylation patterns would not be restored and the only remaining hemi-methylated DNA strands are the ones inherited from the last ancestral cell that was fully ­methylated.

key_points: The recruitment is mediated via JARID2
question: In mammals, how does the histone mark H2Aub (monoubiquitinated histone H2A) contribute to the recruitment of PRC2 to chromatin?
atom_statement: In mammals, the H2Aub histone mark facilitates recruitment of PRC2 via JARID2.
evidence: In contrast to Drosophila, where the role of H2Aub is not well understood, in mammals this mark facilitates recruitment of PRC2 via JARID2.

key_points: They bind to a single nucleosome and reconfigure it

question: What do ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes act on, and what energy source powers the changes they produce?

evidence: Enzymes known as ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes are capable of generating changes by binding to a single nucleosome and reconfiguring it through utilizing the energy obtained from hydrolyzing ATP.

evidence: A shared property of this wide variety of effects rests on a common enzymatic

question:
A purified recombinant human protein is incubated with a DNA substrate containing 5-methylcytosine. Mass spectrometry of the reaction over time shows 5-hydroxymethylcytosine appearing first, followed by 5-formylcytosine and then 5-carboxylcytosine. These products arise from the same cytosine positions, and the protein shows no other DNA-modifying activity.
Is this enzymatic behavior characteristic of a member of the TET protein family (TET1, TET2, TET3)? (Yes/No)
atom_statement: The TET proteins (TET1, TET2, TET3) catalyze the successive oxidation of 5-methylcytosine (5mC) to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), 5-formylcytosine (5fC), and 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC).
evidence: TET2 belongs to a family of three proteins (TET1, TET2, and TET3) that catalyze the successive oxidation of 5-methylcytosine (5meC) to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC), 5-formylcytosine (5fC), and 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC), finally resulting in the replacement of 5meC by an unmodified cytosine (see book 7 Chap. 1 of Wutz).
